passage: At the fish market in Osaka, Aiko, five, held her arms wide. "The fish was THIS big!" she told her friend Yuki, who was the same age. "It was bigger than Papa's suitcase!" Yuki wasn't sure. "How many fish?" Aiko held up three fingers, then five, then changed her mind and counted again on her fingers, whispering numbers. "Three! No, four." Her father laughed quietly behind her. Yuki nodded, believing every word, and spread her own arms wide to show her own fish.

qa.q: How many fish did Aiko finally say she saw?
qa.a: She finally said four fish.

qa.q: What does Aiko's wide arms and changing counts suggest about her feeling?
qa.a: They suggest excitement about the fish, so she stretched the size, not that she meant to mislead. She may also have been unsure of the number.

qa.q: What could Aiko's father do next time she describes something big?
qa.a: He can enjoy the story and ask gentle questions to help her count and compare, without correcting her excitement.

qa.q: How does Yuki seem to take Aiko's story?
qa.a: She believes it and matches it with her own arms, which shows how gestures can carry size before children can measure.

grounding: A child shows size and number with gestures that exaggerate for excitement, before she can measure.

passage: Nursery room note by Preeti. Today at circle time I asked the children how old they were. Jagdish, four, held up four fingers proudly, and then held up five when Riya said she was five. "Me too!" I asked how many biscuits he ate and he held both hands wide and said, "A hundred!" He wasn't trying to fool anyone; he looked delighted. Gestures like these carry numbers before exact counting is learned. I counted with him, using fingers, and he grinned at seeing it was six.

qa.q: How many fingers did Jagdish hold up for his age at first?
qa.a: He held up four fingers.

qa.q: What might Jagdish have been feeling when he said "A hundred!" with both hands wide?
qa.a: He seemed excited and proud about the biscuits, and the number showed how much they meant to him and not an exact count. He might also have wanted to match Riya.

qa.q: How can Preeti help Jagdish with real counting without dampening his joy?
qa.a: She can count with him using fingers and celebrate the real number, as Preeti did.

qa.q: How might Riya see Jagdish's number?
qa.a: She may take it seriously, or she might see he wants to match her, since he changed his fingers to five.

grounding: A child uses finger and arm gestures for number and size, exaggerating from excitement rather than accuracy.

passage: I'm Rekha, from the house by the pond. This morning I saw Yamini come running back from fishing with her grandfather. “Aunty! I caught a fish this big!” She stretched her arms out as wide as they would go, then wider, nearly falling over. Her grandfather held up a small fish, about the size of his palm, and winked at me. Yamini didn't notice. She was jumping. I said, “That's a very big catch!” I don't know if she thought it was really that size, but she was bursting with pride.

qa.q: What did Yamini's grandfather hold up?
qa.a: A small fish, about the size of his palm.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling as she stretched her arms wider and wider?
qa.a: She was excited and proud of her catch, and the wide arms showed how big it felt to her rather than its real size.

qa.q: What was wise about Rekha's reply?
qa.a: Rekha shared Yamini's joy instead of correcting the size, since the gesture was about excitement, not accuracy.

qa.q: How might the grandfather see the arm-spreading?
qa.a: He finds it sweet and funny, which is why he winked at Rekha while holding up the small fish.

grounding: A neighbour observes a child spreading her arms to show a fish's size, exaggerating from excitement rather than accuracy.

passage:
A month before: “How old will you be?” Madhav asked his little sister. Gurpreet held up four fingers, then five, then three, giggling.
A week before: Gurpreet practised with her hand in her lap, folding down her thumb and opening it. “Five!”
Birthday: The guests asked, “How old are you?” Gurpreet held up five fingers proudly. Then she spread her arms wide. “And my cake is THIS big!” Madhav laughed; the cake was only the size of a plate, but it was her favourite.

qa.q: How big was the cake really?
qa.a: Only the size of a plate.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling on her birthday when she spread her arms wide?
qa.a: She was excited and proud, using her arms to show how big her joy felt, not the cake's actual size.

qa.q: What helped Gurpreet show her age correctly?
qa.a: She practised in the weeks before, folding and opening her thumb until five fingers came out right.

qa.q: How does Madhav see Gurpreet's “THIS big” cake?
qa.a: He finds it funny and sweet, knowing the cake is small but that she is excited.

grounding: A preschooler learns to show her age on her fingers over a month and spreads her arms to show excitement about her cake.

passage: The market was loud with sellers shouting, and Shreya had only twenty rupees left. “Ojas, how many balloons?” she asked. He couldn't hear. He held up three fingers, then spread his arms very wide. Shreya bent down. “Three big ones? I only have money for one.” Ojas held up one finger, then slowly brought his arms in to a small circle. “One small one?” He nodded hard. She bought a small red balloon, and Ojas held it like a treasure all the way to the bus.

qa.q: How much money did Shreya have left?
qa.a: Twenty rupees.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he spread his arms very wide?
qa.a: He was excited about the balloons and wanted big ones. Later, bringing his arms in to a small circle showed he accepted one small balloon without getting upset.

qa.q: What did Shreya do well in the noisy market?
qa.a: She bent down, read his finger and arm signs, and said aloud what she understood so they could agree.

qa.q: What would change if the market were quiet?
qa.a: Ojas could have just said what he wanted, but he might still have used his arms to show his excitement.

grounding: A child uses fingers and arm spreads to show number and size in a noisy market, with some excitement-driven exaggeration.

passage:
Back in the colony after the weekend at the lake, Pema stretched her arms as wide as they could go. "The fish was THIS big!"

Kashish laughed. "That's bigger than you!"

"Almost," Pema said. She let her arms come in a tiny bit. "Papa caught it. And we caught more." She held up three fingers, then looked at them, frowned and folded one down. "Two. One jumped back in."

"Was the first one really that big?"

Pema grinned and spread her arms wide again. "Bigger!"

qa.q: How many fingers did Pema hold up at first?
qa.a: Three fingers.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when she spread her arms wide again and said "Bigger!"?
qa.a: She was most likely excited and proud about the fishing trip, and her wide arms showed that excitement more than the fish's real size. She may also have enjoyed teasing Kashish a little.

qa.q: How could an adult respond to Pema's big fish gesture?
qa.a: They could enjoy the excitement with her, and maybe ask something playful, like whether it was bigger than the table, without insisting on exact size.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Pema's story?
qa.a: Kashish finds it funny and doubts the size, laughing that it is bigger than Pema, but still wants to hear more.

grounding: It shows a child using arms and fingers to show size and number, exaggerating the fish to share her excitement.
